headline: Are We Playing God With Genes?
tldr: A geneticist-historian walks through genetics' rare self-imposed research pauses to argue the public, not just scientists, must decide how far gene editing goes.

mindmap.label: As Gods: A Moral History of Genetics
mindmap.note: Matthew Cobb traces genetics' history of self-imposed moratoriums to argue that decisions about gene editing are too important to be left to scientists alone.

children.label: Cobb's path into science history
children.note: A mixed science/humanities education in the UK left him always asking how things got the way they are, not just how they work.

children.label: Studying the maggot's nose
children.note: While researching insect olfaction in France in the mid-90s he found 17th-century references and got hooked on historical research.

children.label: 45 years studying Drosophila
children.note: Nearly 50 years working with fruit flies, understanding genes by mutating them, always wondering what happens if a mutant escapes the lab.

children.label: The four genetics moratoriums
children.note: Cobb frames the book around four unique moments when geneticists voluntarily paused their own research out of fear of what they'd done.

children.label: Unique in the history of science
children.note: No other scientific field, not even the Manhattan Project physicists, has stopped its own work over safety fears.

children.label: 1972 and 1975 Asilomar meetings
children.note: About 200 scientists met at a California cinema to discuss recombinant DNA safety, but only debated 'how,' never 'should we.'

children.label: Self-regulation excluded the public
children.note: NIH funding was tied to biosecurity protocols but had no force of law, and journalists attended but the worried public was never consulted.

children.label: Five years of public protest
children.note: Town hall meetings, notably over Harvard's new lab in Cambridge, Massachusetts, until the controversy evaporated by 1980.

children.label: Fears fizzled, industry boomed
children.note: Human genes in bacteria proved harmless since bacteria can't read human regulatory sequences, and money made the debate go away.

children.label: 1980: Genentech and Apple go public
children.note: Both companies incorporated the same week in Silicon Valley, unknown to each other, marking deregulation-era optimism under Reagan.

children.label: The He Jiankui CRISPR scandal
children.note: A Chinese scientist edited human embryos in 2018, producing three living children with unknown, heritable mutations from a botched experiment.

children.label: Three girls, unknown mutations
children.note: The edited embryos carry mutations never seen in any other human, and not all their cells are affected, risking future well-being.

children.label: Heritable changes are forever
children.note: Because the edits are in reproductive cells, any resulting mutations can pass to all future generations, unlike therapy on an adult's own cells.

children.label: No real medical need existed
children.note: Couples with genetic diseases can already have unaffected biological children via IVF and embryo selection; only a few hundred worldwide truly need embryo editing.

children.label: 'An answer in search of a question'
children.note: Genetic engineer Theodore Friedmann's verdict on human embryo editing: it solves a problem that barely exists.

children.label: No consensus moratorium followed
children.note: Unlike Asilomar, scientists never agreed on a pause; CRISPR co-inventors Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier split, with Charpentier backing a moratorium call and Doudna declining.

children.label: Longtermism and tech-bro futurism
children.note: Cobb pushes back on effective altruists and longtermists who prioritize a distant future humanity over people alive today.

children.label: Elon Musk's Mars fantasy
children.note: Cobb mocks the idea of mutating humans to survive on Mars while working off debt in a 'slave colony.'

children.label: Fix climate and carbon economies instead
children.note: Cobb argues humanity's long-term survival depends on solving climate change, not gene editing, and every country is implicated.

children.label: Gene drives and malaria
children.note: Gene drive technology could spread edited genes uncontrollably through wild populations, raising both huge promise and huge risk.

children.label: 600,000 malaria deaths a year
children.note: Mostly children under five, which is the moral weight scientists working on gene drives carry when weighing the technology's risks.

children.label: Unknown ecological consequences
children.note: Eliminating or altering mosquito populations in a region could have unpredictable ripple effects on ecosystems.

children.label: A simpler alternative: malaria vaccine
children.note: The WHO approved a malaria vaccine that's only 80% effective but could still massively cut transmission without touching mosquito genes.

children.label: Researchers' own fear of gene drives
children.note: Kevin Esvelt, an early gene drive researcher, said he didn't tell his supervisor for a month because he was so frightened by what he'd made.

children.label: Consent problems in Burkina Faso
children.note: Villages where a gene drive trial is planned have no word for 'gene,' so researchers use theater to explain it, yet locals say no one truly asked their consent.

children.label: Mosquitoes ignore borders
children.note: Zika reached Latin America from Africa via ships; mosquitoes breed in stagnant water and travel widely, so one village can't decide alone.

children.label: T-CRISPR in vertebrates
children.note: A new gene drive study, released the same day as the interview, targets invasive house mice in Australia and New Zealand -- the first vertebrate gene drive.

children.label: Who should decide the future
children.note: Cobb calls for public involvement in genetic technology decisions, pointing to aviation and nuclear regulation as models science currently lacks.

children.label: International oversight models
children.note: Cobb proposes something like the civil aviation organization or the International Atomic Energy Agency for global genetic technology regulation.

children.label: Governments lack appetite for regulation
children.note: Cobb doubts governments, especially the US, currently want international regulation of these technologies.

stickies.text: This is too important to be left to the scientists.
600,000 people a year die of malaria, the vast majority children under five.
A gene mutation is forever -- if they have children, those changes will be there.
Human embryo editing is a solution in search of... an answer in search of a question.
He didn't tell his supervisor for a month -- he was so frightened by what he'd made.
Those girls didn't ask how their genes changed -- somebody did it to them.
Nobody asked us -- we don't have any say in this, local women told journalists.
Everything about that experiment in China stank -- there was no medical need.

summary: Matthew Cobb, a zoologist and science historian at the University of Manchester, joins This Week in Science to discuss his book As Gods: A Moral History of the Genetic Age. His interest in blending science and history began with an unusually mixed UK education and deepened while researching insect olfaction in France, where he stumbled on 17th-century texts that hooked him on the field's past. The book's throughline is a striking fact: genetics is the only scientific field where researchers have voluntarily paused their own work, four separate times, out of fear of the consequences.

Cobb walks through the landmark 1972 and 1975 Asilomar meetings, where roughly 200 scientists debated how to safely handle recombinant DNA but never asked whether they should be doing it at all -- and crucially, did so without public input. That self-regulation model, he argues, set a pattern of condescension toward the public that persists today. The controversy faded by 1980 once experiments proved safe and money started flowing, the same year Genentech and Apple both went public.

The conversation turns dark with the 2018 He Jiankui scandal, where a Chinese scientist edited human embryos that became three girls carrying unprecedented, heritable mutations, despite there being no real medical need since existing IVF techniques already let most affected couples have healthy biological children. Cobb calls it a solution in search of a question, criticizing figures like Elon Musk for fantasizing about genetically modifying humans for life on Mars, and notes that even CRISPR's own inventors split on whether a moratorium was warranted.

Gene drives get a nuanced treatment: Cobb refuses to be simply anti-technology, stressing that 600,000 malaria deaths a year, mostly children, are the real stakes, and that researchers pursuing gene drives are thoughtful, not reckless -- one even hid his breakthrough from his supervisor out of fear. But he flags unknown ecological risks, the existence of simpler alternatives like a newly approved malaria vaccine, and a glaring consent problem: villages in places like Burkina Faso have no word for 'gene' yet are expected to approve trials that, given how mosquitoes travel, will affect regions far beyond their borders.

Cobb closes by arguing that genetic technology urgently needs the kind of international oversight aviation and nuclear power already have, but doubts governments currently have the appetite for it. His core message is that history shows genetics' worst fears often didn't come true, but the public was never actually invited to help decide -- and that omission, not the science itself, is the deeper problem.
moves: Read As Gods: A Moral History of the Genetic Age by Matthew Cobb
Look up the He Jiankui CRISPR baby case and its current outcomes
Research the WHO-approved malaria vaccine's real-world rollout and effectiveness
Follow Matthew Cobb (@matthewcobb) for ongoing genetics ethics commentary
Look into gene drive consent debates in Burkina Faso mosquito trials

receipts.title: Genetics uniquely polices itself
receipts.detail: Cobb argues no other scientific field, not even nuclear physics during the Manhattan Project, has ever voluntarily paused its own research out of safety fears -- genetics has done it four times.

receipts.title: Asilomar asked 'how,' never 'should we'
receipts.detail: The famous 1972/75 meetings on recombinant DNA safety were entirely scientist-run and focused only on biosecurity, never on whether the research should happen or including public voices.

receipts.title: The embryo-editing scandal had no real need
receipts.detail: Cobb argues He Jiankui's 2018 experiment served almost no one, since couples with genetic disease can already have healthy biological children via IVF and embryo selection -- true embryo editing might help only a few hundred couples worldwide.

receipts.title: Heritable edits are irreversible
receipts.detail: Unlike therapy on an adult's own cells, editing embryos changes genes that get passed to all future descendants -- a mutation introduced now is, in Cobb's words, forever.

receipts.title: CRISPR's inventors disagreed on a pause
receipts.detail: Emmanuelle Charpentier signed a call for a moratorium on embryo editing; Jennifer Doudna did not, believing it was already too late to stop -- a split Cobb thinks is wrong.

receipts.title: Malaria's death toll frames the gene drive debate
receipts.detail: Cobb insists any discussion of gene drives must start with the fact that roughly 600,000 people, mostly children under five, die of malaria yearly, which is the real cost of inaction.

receipts.title: A researcher was scared of his own invention
receipts.detail: Cobb describes gene drive scientists as deeply conflicted, citing one researcher who felt initial excitement curdle into horror overnight and hid the discovery from his supervisor for a month.

receipts.title: Consent breaks down without shared language
receipts.detail: In proposed Burkina Faso gene drive trials, there's no word for 'gene' in the local language, so researchers use theater to explain the project, yet local women say no one truly asked their permission.

receipts.title: Mosquitoes make consent geographically impossible
receipts.detail: Because mosquitoes travel widely -- Zika reached Latin America from Africa via ships -- a single village cannot meaningfully consent to a gene drive release that will affect a much larger region.

receipts.title: A vertebrate gene drive breakthrough, same-day news
receipts.detail: On the day of the interview, a new study announced the first gene drive in vertebrates, T-CRISPR, aimed at eliminating invasive house mice from Australia and New Zealand.
